Yes, substantially. I believe the aggregate amounts are enormous, relatively at all events, and of course that certainly gives them an inside position which it is going to be very difficult for Canada to meet. We simply cannot meet it if that is to be used as a lever for exports to those countries-purchases by the Latin-American countries.
I wonder how many hon. gentlemen have read Mr. John Gunther's book recently published entitled, "Inside Latin America".
I recommend that book to them. They will find it most interesting reading, and most instructive as well. Those who have read it will have been impressed by the importance
Trade Agreements
placed on trade relationships with the Latin-American countries. Mr. Gunther gives a list of fourteen strategic war materials, indispensable to the conduct of the war, which are not produced in the United States. It may be of interest to list these commodities, only two of which, as I understand, are produced in Canada:
Antimony, chromium, coconut shell char (for gas masks), ferrograde manganese, manila fibre, mercury, mica, nickel, quartz crystal, quinine, rubber, silk, tin, tungsten.
Mr. Gunther further states that Latin. America has surpluses in several of these commodities, and that, with proper development, they could produce them all except silk. Antimony, he states, could be furnished by Mexico and Peru; manganese by Brazil and Cuba; mercury by Mexico; quartz crystal by Brazil; chromium by Cuba; mica by Peru and Chile; tin and tungsten by Bolivia. Coconut shell char could be produced; manila fibre is now being made experimentally in Costa Rica.
I commend that list to the minister; he will read it in Hansard. It may be that some arrangements can be made to increase our imports of these items. He gave a list himself, but I commend this one to -him as having been taken from a source which, I believe, is well informed. It may be of interest to observe that Brazil was once the world's largest producer of rubber, and rubber is, at the moment, a very important element. Indeed, up to fifty or sixty years ago Brazil was, I am informed, the only rubber producing country in the world. It may be that it will become once more a great producer, having regard to the fact that the East Indies plantations are now destroyed or being destroyed. To-day, while rubber trees grow wild over immense areas, I am afraid that production in Brazil has sunk to a low ebb. That, I am told, is because of the competition of the East Indies. With that competition eliminated, it may be possible to revive that production and that export trade. It is said that the President of Brazil is profoundly interested in the resuscitation of the rubber industry and wants to see it developed. There will have to be assistance from the United States and Canada, and with appropriate assistance it might be possible, through such development, to offset any future rubber shortage resulting from the fall of Malaya I offer that, as a constructive suggestion tc the minister and the officials of his depart* ment, for what it is worth.
I direct attention to the productive capacity of the Latin-American countries in these strategic war materials for the reason that il

may be possible to secure from Latin America substitutes for those important raw materials which we can no longer import from the far east. In the meantime one should not forget as well that in Latin America there are other materials produced in which shortages may occur, such as wool, copper and petroleum, and then, of course, Argentina is and has for many years been a great source of supply for the best beef hides in the world, Alberta notwithstanding. The best beef hides come, I am told, from the Argentine.

I do not pretend to give the reason, but that is what tanners and importers have told me. There was a time when these hides were imported direct into Fredericton and turned into sole leather, but like many other maritime industries it has been absorbed by central Canada. We buy our sole leather pretty largely from Ontario, and that is a pity, because we should be able to manufacture it ourselves, though they tell me that they cannot profitably compete because consumption is so low. However, that is just a matter in passing. I commend these suggestions to the minister; and I hope the officials of the government, if they do me the honour of reading them, will explore- perhaps in consultation with officials of the United States government-the possibility of increasing the productive capacity of South American countries in these essential war supplies.	_	,
I wish to turn now to a brief consideration of the extension of our trade with South America both now and in the post-war period. As I mentioned earlier, the former trade relations of South America were largely with Europe. These have now ceased. I believe that in the post-war period) Canada should make a most aggressive attempt to sell manufactured goods as well as raw materials and the products of agriculture, particularly flour, seed potatoes and other things we can produce in quantities for export. No better seed potatoes are grown anywhere in this northern hemisphere than those produced in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. Our farmers are restricted in a degree in their exports to the United States, and they have to meet the competition of the seed potatoes produced in Aroostook county, which, as everyone knows, is a very large producer. But quality counts, and our producers have the quality; there is no doubt about that. The cleanest seed potato fields on this continent are found first, I think, in Prince Edward Island, and second in New Brunswick. The hon. member for Yictoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) shakes his head. I suppose he would 
reverse the order, and perhaps I should place them at least on an equal plane. But the question of plant disease is important in that regard, and of course we must send out the very best quality that can be obtained. There is a very large market for seed potatoes in South America if the proper transportation and exchange facilities can be arranged.
I should like to say to the Minister that within the last few weeks the whole thing has been hampered by the controls that now exist. Export licences and all that sort of thing have a hampering effect on that trade, which is a very desirable trade indeed. The minister said it was paid for in United States dollars, which is correct. That is important from another standpoint; and I hope that officialdom-I am not using that word in any derogatory sense at all-will make it as easy as possible to send these things to South America. I recommend to the minister that his department give some attention to this question of cramping regulations and restrictions on a trade that ought to be as free as it is possible to make it, for the good not only of our producers but of trade relationships generally between this country and South America. I am not going to particularize further.
Prior to the war, all the Latin-American countries imported large quantities of manufactured goods from Europe. That resulted more or less from very intelligent trade direction, especially on the part of Germany. I believe it should be possible for us, pursuing the good neighbour policy, to gain at least, a portion of this market for Canadian manufacturers in the post-war period. There is the difficulty of United States competition, of course. If we could accomplish this, together with the export of natural products, we would be taking a long step toward providing for the readjustment of war industries to a peace-time basis, thereby providing employment for our workmen. I am speaking now of the post-war period. These are the things to which we ought to be looking forward, trying to get as many new markets as we can to take up the slack which will be created when we change back from a war-time activity to a peace-time economy. We cannot afford to forget for a moment that this transition is coming. There need not be a depression if officialdom and business will get together and plan ahead, and I recommend constant study in that regard.	*
I have referred already to the difficulties in connection with trading with South America resulting from the fact that we have no direct trade routes. Has the minister given any attention or thought to this point? It is not possible at the moment to establish direct trade routes; I am quite sure the shipping is

Trade Agreements
not available. Any shipping that we are building will have to go to replace the shipping being lost in the Atlantic, and for transatlantic trade; but some of that shipping might be diverted to the South American trade. Certainly some of the cargo ships that Canada is building can be diverted to the South American trade after the war is over, and I commend that suggestion to the minister. Perhaps as the result of our merchant shipping programme and our great naval expansion we may become once more in the post-war period what we were a generation or more ago, a great mercantile marine nation. I am sure that is what the people of the maritime provinces would like to see happen. Then we may be able to establish for ourselves direct shipping routes to all the important countries in the world, including those of South America.
Unless in future we are able to establish direct trade routes I fear that it will not be possible to extend our trade with the Latin-American countries in the manner we would all like, particularly because of the competition with the United States. These particular trade agreements to which the minister has alluded, especially the three that are before us, the result of the visit to South America by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his party last autumn, constitute a step in the right direction. By securing for ourselves most-favoured-nation treatment in the markets of Argentina, Brazil and Chile, subject to certain small limitations, as I understood from the minister's statement, I am hopeful that at last an initial step has been taken to extend our trade with these countries.
I should like to have some enlightenment from the minister on one particular matter in connection with the most-favoured-nation treatment. I note that the advantages accorded to Canada do not carry with them the advantages which in one instance Chile accords to Argentina, Bolivia and Peru, and which in another instance Argentina accords, to Bolivia, Chile, Paraguay and Uruguay, and again which Brazil accords to contiguous countries. The minister may have covered that point fully; I was not able to follow him. I think he did refer to these matters, but perhaps at a later stage he would be good enough to state succinctly just what the effect of these exceptions from most-favoured-nation treatment will be upon our trade.
I would ask the minister, also, to tell us in what particular lines it is anticipated that our trade with the three countries will be extended as a result of these agreements. In what particular lines does the according of the mostfavoured-nation treatment give to Canadian products favourable tariff status, so that
increased exports are likely to result? I believe he might also give us a statement as to what tariff barriers are to be surmounted.
In the agreements with Argentina and Brazil I note that certain articles provide that prohibition or restriction may be imposed for the protection of plants and animals, and that measures for protection against disease, degeneration or extinction, as well as measures taken against harmful seeds, plants or animals are not to be affected. Presumably this provision is directed against certain Canadian commodities which might be exported to these countries. I should like to have that position elucidated.
I should hope that these countries will not use these provisions to declare prohibitions. We have a classic illustration of that in connection with the export of potatoes from Canada to Great Britain. They are adamant against importing any of our potatoes in a commercial way because of the presence in Canada, they allege, of the Colorado beetle. Of course that is a terrible pest, and costs the farmers of this country vast sums of money each year. Not only do they lose a large sum of money, but the presence of the beetle causes a great deal of labour.
I am afraid, however, that agricultural communities in the old country have used the beetle as-I shall not say a pretext, but as a means of excluding our potatoes from Great Britain. I have never thought that that was cricket.
I have very little more to say to the minister. I was interested, however, to learn that he spent some time in Chile. I suppose it was not within the ambit of his mission to inquire what Chile was going to do about the service of her external debt. There are many Canadian nationals who bought Chile bonds in days gone by, and who would like to have some interest on those bonds.

Mr. Speaker, I have neither the qualifications nor the background of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) or the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) to take part in this debate. I have, however, given some attention to these matters for a number of

years, and I accept the invitation of the leader of the opposition to offer some comment.
When the minister began his mission in 1940, as he related to the house he took ill, and there was considerable criticism in various parts of the country to the effect that the minister's illness ought not to have precluded the progress of the mission. I believe it should be said here-and I suggest anyone who knows Latin America will agree-that to have sent anyone other than a minister, and particularly the minister of this department, as head of the delegation, would have been a great mistake.

speechtext: I agree.

speechtext:
The minister has paid
appropriate tributes to certain officials in his department. I should like to pay my tribute to a friend of mine who did considerable work, not under governmental but under private auspices. I refer to Mr. Ronald McEaehren of the Financial Post in Toronto, a paper with which I cannot always say I am in full accord. I feel, however, that special reference should be made to Mr. McEachren's work. He went to the various Latin-American countries, and did a great deal af advance work of his own which has proved to be of incalculable value. That fact is apparent to anyone who reads business journals, and particularly those in the South American countries.
The discussion thus far has been largely confined to the economic aspect of the problem which, I venture to suggest to the minister, is by no means the important one. To illustrate my meaning in that connection I purpose bringing out into relief, but with a different emphasis and consideration in mind, some of the figures the minister and the leader of the opposition have discussed.
The minister's figures dealt essentially with six countries. There are at least ten countries which, I suggest, should be characterized as being among the most important ones, and whose trade figures must be related, if this discussion is to receive the complete coverage it deserves. The two important countries, per se and in respect of our relations with them are, first Brazil, and then Argentina.
In 1939 Brazil imported from Canada goods to the value of about $4,406,789. That importation made Brazil in that year our chief Latin-American customer. Argentina was next with an importation of about $4,116,923. In 1940-and I am taking these three years because I believe they tell a very interesting story-Argentina took first position, with purchases from Canada amounting to some $6,000,215. representing a 40 per cent increase

over the previous year, made up chiefly of imports of newsprint. In the same year Brazil increased her imports to a sum of $5,062,000. In 1941 Brazil continued to increase her imports. In that year they reached a total value of about $8,097,143, while those of Argentina fell back into second position, with a total importation from us of about $7,172,104.
Our imports during these three years from the two countries named are significant. In 1939 we purchased goods to the value of $1,111,291 from Brazil, and from Argentina $4,406,456. In 1940 we bought from Argentina $8,541,S62, and from Brazil about $6,243,342, a slightly smaller amount.
In 1941 we bought from Argentina goods valued at $4,763,752, and from Brazil we almost. doubled our imports. In that year we imported a value of $19,443,946.
These figures yield but one conclusion-and I do not say this by way of any criticism of our trade commissioners-but the fact remains that two years of war have brought more for us by way of increased trade from Latin America to us, and from us to Latin America, than did fifteen years of good, energetic and efficient work by our trade commissioners. I do not want to criticize what the minister has done because his work in this particular has been of tremendous advantage to our country, particularly in respect of the political relations of this part of North America with Latin America, but the fact is that the trade figures are not impressive. For instance, in 1939 our exports to South America were only 1-8 per cent of our total exports, and our imports from South America in the same year were but 2-8 per cent of our total imports. When you compare that with our trade with all of North America, excluding the United States, where our exports amounted to 2-9 per cent of our total exports and our imports to 2-3 per cent of our total imports, you will realize that trade between Canada and the United States is more important to the United States than the whole Latin-American trade carried on by that country. There are reasons for these relatively unimportant trade balances, reasons which in former days parliament has not frankly considered.

suggest one reason? It has always been an astonishing thing to me that our trade commissioners are not and never have been what I heard one Minister of Trade and Commerce indignantly deny that they were, commercial travellers.

The leader of the opposition, having been Minister of Trade and Commerce,

Trade Agreements
is more expert in that particular than I am. I was glad to hear his speech to-day, particularly bearing in mind that he spoke on behalf of the Conservative party. I know something about Latin America. I well remember a speech delivered in this house by the former able member for St. Lawrence-St. George. That gentleman had had considerable experience with Latin Americans and he characterized them as people who were hardly civilized, as people with whom we should not try to cultivate any relations. That has been the impression which many Canadians, generally and officially, have had about Latin America, and perhaps the Latin Americans have had somewhat the same impression about us. The time has come, with the world in its present dire straits, w'hen we can no longer take that view of these other twenty-one countries who share our American continental interest.
I would not for a moment suggest that we cannot find increasing opportunities for trade with Latin America, but I do believe that we are overemphasizing and have overemphasized the importance of our trade in the past and the possibilities of our trade in the future, for various reasons, some of which were set out by the leader of the opposition. It is possible that we may increase Canada's imports of linseed, fruits, hides and wool from Latin America, and we may sell them more lumber, newsprint, machinery, textiles, fish and perhaps some wheat to Peru. But the fact is, as the leader of the opposition has mentioned, we must compete in the Latin-American countries with the United States with its lower costs because of mass production and its added advantage because of having been in these markets long before we thought of getting into them. There have also been huge extensions of credits by the United States to Latin America. Then there is the further fact that our economy is competitive with Latin-American countries, rather than complementary. Some of the things that are basic in their national income are basic in ours, and this presents additional difficulties.
As far as tropical products are concerned, a large part of our supplies come to us under preferential agreements from the British West Indies and British Guiana. Even though a movement has been set on foot in the course of the last few days, particularly in Washington, for the general lowering of tariff barriers, I venture to suggest by way of qualification of what the leader of the opposition has said that in the post-war period we shall find it to our essential interest to recover established channels of exchange with Europe; not that we should not try to increase our trade opportunities in Latin America, but because we are an exporting nation, because thirty per cent of our income is based upon what we sell to other nations of the world. Because of our competitive position with the United States we should not forget our normal channels of exchange.
It is true, and I should have said this earlier, that the future may have great opportunities for this country in the Caribbean and in South America, particularly as a result of recent capital expansion on the part of the United States. The anticipated increases in the nutritional standards of many Latin-American countries, together with the consequential increase in the standards of living, may conceivably change the market potentialities for Canada in Latin America. But I think it is safe to say that the strictest analysis of our trade possibilities by those who are specialists in these matters indicates the impossibility of our ever getting into the position of hemispheric self-sufficiency in the economic sense.
I said a moment ago that one of the reasons for our relatively unimportant trade increases in Latin America was our lack of appreciation of Latin America itself. As the leader of the opposition has said, one of our most important contacts with Latin America is the mining, power and traction enterprises which are financed by Canadian capital in Mexico, Brazil, Peru and Colombia. Yet the most serious criticisms of Latin Americans and their ways have come from Canadians who draw dividends from these companies.
I do not wish to emphasize the economic aspects so much, although they are important, as to suggest that we should give attention to the penetration of nazi influence into almost every country of Latin America. This penetration has been by way of subventions to industry and subsidies to air companies, and a situation was created which caused the greatest alarm on the part of the United States and Great Britain. One might well ask where we who are fighting Germany to-day would be were it not for the good-neighbour policy of the United States and Latin America, to which policy we as a nation have made very little contribution. Consequently in analysing our opportunities in this respect we must bear in mind not only our economic position but particularly our political opportunities with Latin America. I do not think I am expressing far-fetched views or stretching the bounds of relevancy when I suggest that the conclusions reached at Ogdensburg by the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) can be considered to
Trade Agreements

be related to this whole problem; for the report given out jointly by the President of the United States and our Prime Minister on the Ogdensubrg agreement included this phraseology, that the permanent board was to: -commence immediate studies relating to sea, land and air problems including personnel and material, and to consider in a broad sense the defence of the north half of the western hemisphere.
The north half of the western hemisphere may include the south side of the Panama canal or it may merely embrace the north side, but I do submit that this important statement made on behalf of our two countries has a definite relation to the problem under discussion. The area covered by the understandings or conclusions reached at Ogdensburg includes the north American Republics of Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama; the republics and colonies in the Caribbean, and Colombia, Venezuela, the Guianas and parts of Brazil and Ecuador in South America. Thus it includes the whole of the greater Panama canal zone, which according to the very text referred to by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), namely, Mr. Gunther's work, would be that part of America where the nazis would be more likely than not to exercise mischief.
Our interest in the defence of the canal is not less than that of the United States, although we traditionally seem to regard it as out of our sphere; for the canal is the shortest ocean route between our eastern and western provinces. The canal also affords the quickest means of ocean communication from our western ports to the European market, upon which we are more dependent than even the United States.
I am not suggesting or trying to read into these treaties or into the Ogdensburg conversations something that was not contemplated, but it may be that we are unconsciously, and I think properly, drifting into an orbit where there are at stake economic interests for this country, and more particularly that there lies an opportunity of recognizing that in Latin America exists the only contemporary collectivity of nations outside of the British commonwealth whereby there can be some guarantee of peaceful relations between states. There has been great difficulty in the past in discussing this subject in the house. Closer relations with Latin America have always been construed by many as an attempt to weaken the ties we have with the United Kingdom and the British empire, just as attempts to bring about closer relationship between Canada and the United States have often been similarly construed. Surely the fact that to-day twenty-one of the South American and Central American republics have recently severed connections

with the axis powers, in spite of nazi influence in those countries during the past six years, indicates that it is up to us, not only unconsciously but consciously, to go about to identify our position in Latin America-not thereby weakening our relationships with Great Britain or the British commonwealth, but just as our friendship with the United States has brought Britain and the United States closer together, we might as a result of our more active participation in the whole matter of hemispheric defence, viewed economically and politically, bring Britain, the United States and ourselves and the Latin-American countries closer and closer together in respect of the period of postwar reconstruction.
Why should this not be done? While there is some denial in pan-American countries of the democratic process and of the principle of due process of law, there is nevertheless a general sympathy with the democratic method. In the whole system of collective organization as we have it in the pan-American system there is a recognition of racial equality, an acknowledgment of the desirability of preserving the democratic processes. We find there in almost every national instance a respect for religious beliefs. Is there not there an indication such as we have had recently at Rio de Janeiro that there can be cooperation, and effective cooperation, between one nation and another? Do these nations not have respect for treaties?
It seems to me therefore, Mr. Speaker, that we have every bond with these peoples. We want not only to increase our trade with them but to go along generally with them and, as the leader of the opposition said, build a stronger world politically [DOT] in the interests of civilization and decency. To the extent that these treaties are a step in that direction, I compliment the minister and the government upon their efforts. I am sure that the house, if given the opportunity, would want this discussion to go down as indicating to the people in what I might call the unknown countries south of the Rio Grande that we regard them to be civilized men and women and members of nations with whom we would like to enjoy the most friendly relations, and that we propose in the future to perpetuate our economic and political relations with them to our mutual advantage.

subtopic: CHILE, BRAZIL, AND THE ARGENTINE-MOTIONS FOR APPROVAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have enjoyed greatly the speeches which have been delivered thus far. I feel that it is in order to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and his party on what I believe was a fine piece of work. Inasmuch as the minister himself accorded to the Prime Minis-

Trade Agreements
tor (Mr. Mackenzie King) a good deal of the credit in this connection, I should like to pass along a similar tribute to him too.
I enjoyed the contribution of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and the contribution of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), who always speaks in this chamber with moderation and with evidence of scholarship and good judgment.
With respect to the measures now before us,
I believe that they deserve our hearty approval. It seems to me that judged from almost every point of view, these agreements are highly commendable. It is true that we need particularly at this time good-will in the hearts of as many peoples as possible, and it surely does seem difficult to conceive why good-will should not be engendered first in the hearts of our neighbours, and our nearest neighbours. The Latin-American people are surely our neighbours.
It is well, I think, that all the goods listed as being contemplated for exchange between Canada and the South American countries named are goods, first of all, which we need from them, and second, goods which do not compete with our own.	I consider it an
unwise tendency in any state to endeavour to leave its own industries unprotected, to throw them open to competition with goods coming from abroad. It therefore is an important matter that these goods do not, as it appears, compete with Canadian goods.
Now, the goods which we are to export are goods which we can spare. I believe that for many years we have been neglectful of our own people. The first duty of Canada with respect to her production is to see to it that her own people have their needs supplied. Many times in the past we have thought first of all of the goods which we could sell abroad, not bothering much about the people at home-very much as our fathers on the farms used to sell the marketable eggs and keep the poor ones for the family to eat. That was good management in those trying times, but I am not sure that it is good management nationally.
Another thing which appeals to me in connection with this treaty is that very few other nations wish to export the particular goods which we propose to export. I believe that long before this parliament finishes we shall be engaged in earnest discussions of the causes of war. It ought to be borne in on every hon. member that one of the greatest causes of war is the attempt on the part of one nation to force its goods into markets which it does not need in order to live, thereby excluding from those markets similar goods from other nations that need to sell in
those markets to live. No offence is committed in this treaty in relation to that important matter. Therefore we can say that Canada, in enjoying these treaties, will not be excluding others from needed markets, will not be depriving others of enjoyment.
Another aspect of these agreements which commends itself to members of my group is the tendency to give favoured nation treatment in so far as that means a lowering of tariffs. It may be difficult for people who think along lines which Conservatives habitually follow to conceive of lowering tariffs and at the same time protecting home industry. It must be understood-it must come to be understood-that there are ways of protecting the home industry other than the raising of a tariff barrier, which increases the price to everyone in the country. It is completely possible to protect our own industry by special favours conferred upon our industry. For example, by using the national credit of a country it is completely possible- has been proved so in the world time and again during the last ten years-to lower the costs of production, to decrease the costs of freight, and to discount the price of the commodity as it comes to the consumer. If such a series of devices be used within the state it is completely possible to lower the tariff and still protect home industries. Since that is so I commend this tendency toward lower tariffs.
I believe I have said all that at this time we feel disposed to say. We commend the treaties.

subtopic: CHILE, BRAZIL, AND THE ARGENTINE-MOTIONS FOR APPROVAL
speechtext:
These treaties have had a sufficiently long discussion this afternoon and little more needs to be said. I rise simply to say that we of this group are in favour of every treaty and every move that can be made to bring about better relations, both commercial and social, across the world.
I should like to emphasize one point. In our relationships with our South American neighbours the time has come when we ought to join with them in the pan-American conference. I am British-born and therefore I have naturally a great regard and love for the old land. But I can see no reason in the world why this country should not realize its geographical, economic and commercial position and enter into the closest relationships possible with our neighbours across the line, and with our neighbours, rather more remote, in South America. It would be good for the world, for Britain, for Canada, for all of us; and I hope that as these trading relationships are promoted, as these treaties go into effect, the government will fill that vacant seat at
Labour Conditions

the pan-American conference and assist our good neighbour to the south in bringing about still better relationships between the Anglo-Saxon and Latin-American peoples.
After all that has been said in praise of the treaties, nothing much remains for me to say. We approve them. We hope they are a forerunner of future trade relationships in ever-widening fields; and we give the adoption of these treaties our whole-hearted support.
On motion of Mr. Stirling the debate was adj ourned.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext:
I thought I ought to bring at once to the attention of the house a decision which the government made to-day with reference to the situation in British Columbia and the evacuation of persons of Japanese origin in that province.
All hon. members, I am sure, realize what an enormous undertaking the moving of large numbers of persons from their homes to other parts of the country really is, and how many are the considerations of which account must be taken in a transaction of great magnitude, particularly where it has to be carried out expeditiously. We have felt that it would be helpful in every way to the province of British Columbia, in meeting the situation, if we were to associate with the government's effort prominent citizens of the province itself so that they might bring their combined knowledge of affairs in the province to bear on the carrying out of the various projects which it will be necessary to undertake in evacuating this large number of people. The government therefore has decided to appoint what will be designated the British Columbia security commission. The present intention is to have three members, all of whom will
be persons outstanding in the province. The government has asked Mr. Austin Taylor if he would act as chairman of the commission and he has expressed his willingness to accept the position. The commission will be for the purpose of directing and supervising the evacuation of persons of Japanese origin from protected areas to the particular localities to which they will be sent. The commission will have to do with the transportation, placement, accommodation and so on of the different persons who are to be evacuated. The government itself will continue to do all that it is doing and had planned to do, but the work will be carried out in association with, and more particularly under the direction of the commission. Every agency of government that can be of service to that >ody will be asked to assist in helping to perform this large undertaking in a manner that will serve to occasion the least irritation among those who are being transferred, and in a manner which will help to give the citizens of British Columbia the most in the way of essential security. All that can be done by government departments will be carried out through that agency.
I thought it advisable to make this statement at once in order that the citizens of British Columbia may know of the government's purpose in the matter. The order in council appointing the commission has not yet been passed, but in all probability will be passed to-morrow.

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext: In that connection may I ask whether this security commission will have any power to settle evacuees outside the province, or is it the intention that they shall simply be moved from one part of the province to another? There is also another question. In this evening's Ottawa newspapers there is a news dispatch to the effect that there has been an amendment made to the defence of Canada regulations providing that the Japanese may not possess motor vehicles and other articles. Has that order been passed within the last day or two and, if so, could we have the details?

As I understand it, the
powers of the commission have not yet been defined conclusively; the matter is still in the making. Hon. L. S. St. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, the defence of Canada regulations were amended to empower the Minister of Justice to make certain orders with respect to all persons ordinarily resident in a protected area. That order in council was tabled here on Wednesday of this week. There has been an amendment to the defence of Canada regulations to authorize the enforcement of such orders as may be made by the Minister of Justice, not only by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police but by any police officer, provincial or municipal, in the area affected. I should like to table a copy of that order and to suggest that perhaps it might be printed, as were the others, in the Votes and Proceedings.
Following that, there was made by the Minister of Justice an order dated February 26, 1942, which I also table and suggest that it be included in the Votes and Proceedings.

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext: To what does that relate?

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext:
That is the order dealing first of all with the curfew imposed upon all persons of Japanese origin; an order that all persons of Japanese origin give up all motor vehicles, cameras, radio transmission or receiving sets, firearms, ammunition and so forth; that they be required forthwith to deliver up these articles to the nearest justice of the peace or peace officer, and that he be required to give a receipt for the article delivered to him and immediately notify the Royal Canadian Mounted Police of the receipt of such article by him. The order also provides that every person of the Japanese race shall leave a protected area forthwith. That is completed by the terms of the regulation itself, which provide that any person in any protected area reasonably believed by any peace officer or by any person acting on behalf of his majesty to be contravening the regulation may, without prejudice to other proceedings, be removed from the protected area or detained therein by any peace officer or person acting on behalf of his majesty as aforesaid. Therefore the order made by the Minister of Justice, and the
regulations, provide that from now on it is an offence against the regulation for any person of Japanese origin to be outside his premises between dusk and dawn. It is an offence for him to retain possession of a motor car, explosives, or one of the other objects enumerated. It is an offence for him to be within a protected area, and for any such offence he may be removed from the area, or detained by any peace officer. Instructions were immediately given for carrying out these provisions, through the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and in cooperation with provincial and municipal police in British Columbia.
The instructions provide, of course, that with respect to the removal of persons of Japanese origin there will have to be priorities. They cannot all be moved at the same moment, and for that purpose instructions are to be taken from the chiefs of the army, navy and air services, as to which are the most urgent cases. Males of sixteen years and upward will be and are being dealt with just as quickly as provision can be made to house them.
The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) has been kind enough to call my attention to what was regarded as some conflict respecting the orders of February 24, as reported in Votes and Proceedings. I think the hon. member will agree, upon looking at them, that there is no real conflict. The one order which is generally applicable to the whole of Canada prevents the acquisition of land or crops by a person of Japanese origin. That contains provision that it does not apply to the taking by lease of buildings for a period of not more than one year.
It was believed that when these people had to leave protected areas it might be possible for them to take short-term leases of buildings for their own accommodation, pending some other arrangement. It is now represented that there may be areas outside the protected areas where they should not be allowed even to do that.

Where
they are not wanted.

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS

speechtext:
Yes, and where there would be unusual reasons for not wanting them. I should not imagine there would be many areas in Canada where there would be an active desire to acquire them.
On that point I wish to assure the hon. member that we shall welcome any suggestion, and that these orders may have to be further extended. Any suggestion made will receive very careful consideration, because it is the desire of the department to have these orders in form such as adequately to cope with the situation.
Japanese Nationals

Hon. GiROTE STIRLING (Yale): Mr. Speaker, if I might be permitted, under these unusual circumstances, I should like to make one or two comments. The minister has been good enough to explain to me some of the conditions under which this new order is being issued. I note that it applies not only to nationals, as did the previous order, but to those of Japanese origin. They are to move forthwith.
It appears to me not improbable that this may start something in the nature of a flood. I want to warn the government once more that if the representations and protests from the part of British Columbia which I represent are not heeded, and these people are allowed to filter in and to settle for a temporary period, even under lease, I am very much afraid there will be grave trouble.

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the minister. I understood him' to say that those Japanese in areas considered most vital are to be moved. My understanding is that the first Japanese to be moved are the Japanese nationals. My question is: Will Japanese be moved from vital areas, such as power plants, irrespective of their nationality?

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext: Yes; those to be first moved will be moved having respect to the area. The various departments of national defence are to indicate which areas they consider specially vulnerable, and all persons of Japanese origin are to be moved from those areas as quickly as possible.

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext: They will be the first moved?

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext: Yes; they will be the first ones moved.

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA SECURITY COMMISSION- EVACUATION FROM PROTECTED AREAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make some comment respecting the point raised by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), and would suggest that we have to be reasonable. If we are going to put the onus on the government-and it will have to be put on the government-of removing these people from areas in which it is dangerous to leave them, we must remember that they must be settled somewhere. There is an obligation upon the government to find a place to put them. There is also an obligation upon hon. members to assist the government in finding that place. Otherwise there is no rhyme or reason to the attitude we take.

subtopic: JAPANESE NATIONALS

We have done that.
